analysis.one_liner: Restores the right to sue pesticide makers in state court over inadequate label warnings.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, where it received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that federal pesticide law blocks state lawsuits over pesticide warning labels, ending a common way for people injured by pesticides to win compensation. This bill would change federal law to say those state lawsuits are still allowed, and it would require the EPA to report on any of its rules that limit such claims. It was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors and referred to the Agriculture Committee, where it went no further.
analysis.who_benefits: People who believe they were harmed by pesticide exposure—such as users of herbicides like Roundup who developed cancer—would regain the ability to sue manufacturers in state court for failing to warn, a path the Supreme Court closed in Monsanto v. Durnell [S2]. Their families and communities would also benefit from stronger accountability pressure on manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: It amends FIFRA so that federal law can no longer be read to block state tort claims over pesticide labeling or packaging, letting injured people sue manufacturers in state court.

It clarifies that a warning required under a state's tort law may be placed on a pesticide label, addressing the problem the Supreme Court created in Monsanto v. Durnell, where a federal label without a cancer warning defeated a state verdict.
It directs EPA to report within 180 days on any of its rules or guidance that restrict state tort claims, and to say what steps it took to bring those into compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would bear the cost of more litigation and potentially expanded warning labels. Those costs could partly flow through to farmers and consumers as higher prices [S2].

drawbacks.text: Allowing state-by-state warning requirements could expose pesticide makers to a patchwork of labeling obligations and litigation costs across states, an expense that could be passed on to farmers and food prices.

Opponents of liability under state law argue that EPA-approved federal labels are the appropriate national standard and that bypassing preemption creates conflicting safety determinations; the bill's findings dispute this by citing EPA's reliance on conditional registrations and outdated science [S2], but the counterargument remains the industry's core case against the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—restoring a practical path to compensation for people harmed by pesticides after the Supreme Court closed off state failure-to-warn claims—could be substantial for affected individuals and would add pressure on EPA to use current science. The costs fall on pesticide manufacturers, who face more litigation and labeling uncertainty, and those costs could be passed to farmers through higher prices. The bill had no cosponsors and sat in committee, so its prospects were poor; a sincere objection is that patchwork state labeling warnings could complicate a federal registration system, though the bill's premise is that the federal system has failed to protect people on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, got no cosponsors, and never moved before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 24, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture.
It drew no cosponsors in the House.
No further action—no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration—was taken after the referral.

The bill responded to the Supreme Court's June 2026 Monsanto v. Durnell decision, which held that federal pesticide law barred a state failure-to-warn claim where EPA approved the label without a cancer warning.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers are better off: they keep federal preemption as a defense against state lawsuits, while people harmed by pesticide exposure have no legal recourse restored.

for.name: Rep. Nancy Mace
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to preserve state tort claims against pesticide manufacturers.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or floor consideration.

against.name: Pesticide industry
against.what_they_did: Have lobbied for federal preemption of state pesticide labeling lawsuits, the very doctrine this bill would roll back.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, sponsored the bill and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan breakdown is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Pesticide manufacturers (e.g., makers of Roundup/glyphosate products)
industries.note: The bill strips away federal preemption as a shield in state tort suits, exposing manufacturers to failure-to-warn litigation like the $1.25 million verdict the Supreme Court overturned in Monsanto v. Durnell [S2]. Manufacturers could face more lawsuits and pressure to add warning labels.

The bill does not reform EPA registration itself—including the roughly 65 percent of pesticides approved through conditional registration [S2]—it only adds a state-law backstop, leaving the federal approval system intact.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and has sat in the Agriculture Committee since August 2026 with no action; at this level of support, the realistic path is that it dies in committee when this Congress ends.
